content.title: About
content.content: The chicken deli sandwich with cheese is a classic sub made with tender slices of seasoned chicken breast, melted cheese, fresh vegetables, and sauce, served on a soft roll. It is offered at restaurant #1762.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Deli‑style chicken is usually marinated in a blend of herbs and spices, giving it a distinctive flavor.
Chicken sandwiches are a popular quick‑lunch or snack option in fast‑food and café menus.
The cheese can be either processed or a firm variety, depending on the establishment’s preference.
The roll is typically soft with a lightly crisp exterior, providing a pleasant texture contrast.
Restaurant #1762 is known for its focus on ingredient quality and freshness.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides a high‑quality source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, which supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, chicken breast contains less saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is rich in B6 and B12 vitamins, which aid nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Nutrient‑rich vegetables
items.content: Fresh veggies contribute fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy protein sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Marinades and sauces can be high in salt, which is a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage of chicken can lead to growth of pathogenic bacteria.

items.title: Gluten in the roll
items.content: For those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity, the roll may pose a problem.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be enjoyed hot or cold, sliced in half. It pairs well with fries, a side salad, or a light dip. Add extra sauce or spices to taste if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in plastic film. Keep the roll in a separate container to prevent sogginess. Reheat in an oven or grill to retain a crisp crust.

chicken-or-turkey-garden-salad-chicken-a.title: Garden Salad with Chicken or Turkey

content.title: About
content.content: The garden salad contains boiled chicken or turkey breast, fresh lettuce leaves, cucumber, bell pepper, radish and green onion. It is prepared without tomatoes, carrots or dressing, making it a light, low‑calorie dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are excellent sources of lean protein, suitable for low‑fat diets.
No dressing preserves the natural flavors of the vegetables and meat.
The salad can be assembled in 10‑15 minutes, ideal for quick work lunches.
Bell pepper is rich in vitamin C, which enhances iron absorption from the meat.
Radish provides antioxidants and a mild peppery bite.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey supply high‑quality protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Lean poultry contains little saturated fat, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is a good source of vitamin B6 and niacin, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Fiber and micronutrients
items.content: Vegetables add dietary fiber, vitamin C, potassium and folate, promoting digestion and immunity.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Absence of dressing and use of lean meat make the dish suitable for weight management.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing skin reactions or digestive issues.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor salmonella or campylobacter; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If using pre‑cooked meat, check sodium levels to avoid excess salt intake.

items.title: Nutrient interactions
items.content: Large protein portions can reduce plant‑based iron absorption; pair with vitamin C to compensate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad cold or slightly chilled. It can be eaten on its own, packed in a lunch box, or used as a filling for wraps. If desired, drizzle a small amount of olive oil and lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, separate the meat from the vegetables to prevent leaf wilting.

classic-mixed-vegetables-canned-cooked-n.title: Classic Mixed Vegetables, Canned, Cooked, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Classic mixed vegetables are a canned blend of carrots, corn, peas, and green beans that are cooked without any added fat. The vegetables are blanched, sealed in airtight cans, and heat‑sterilized to preserve flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix typically includes 4–5 vegetable varieties, providing a range of textures and tastes.
Being fat‑free makes the product low‑calorie and suitable for weight‑management diets.
Rapid thermal processing retains most B‑vitamins and carotenoids.
The product is popular in military rations and backpacking meals because of its long shelf life.
Cans are coated internally to prevent metal leaching.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes it appropriate for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, while vitamin C aids the immune system.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene and other phytochemicals protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: A brine may be used for preservation; individuals monitoring sodium intake should be aware.

items.title: Allergy to individual vegetables
items.content: Some people may be allergic to carrots, peas, or corn.

items.title: Bacterial contamination if the can is damaged
items.content: Bulging or dented cans can harbor pathogens and should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The vegetables can be eaten straight from the can, added to soups, stews, salads, or used as a side dish for meat. They can also be quickly warmed in a pan with herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts are a legume whose seeds are commonly referred to as nuts. Native to South America, they are now cultivated in warm regions worldwide. Peanuts have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. They can be eaten raw, roasted, salted, or processed into peanut butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts belong to the legume family, not true nuts, though they are treated as nuts in cooking.
There are several varieties: smooth, runner, Virginia, and Spanish peanuts.
Peanuts were introduced to Africa and Asia by European colonists in the 16th–17th centuries.
They are used to make peanut butter, pastes, sauces, confectionery, and even flour.
Peanut plants fix nitrogen, improving soil fertility.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, making them a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat in peanuts is monounsaturated and polyunsaturated, which support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts provide niacin, folate, and thiamine, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They contain magnesium, phosphorus, iron, and zinc, which aid bone health and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Peanuts contain resveratrol and phenolic compounds that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common allergens; reactions can be severe.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Peanuts are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Aflatoxins
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold producing aflatoxins, which are harmful to the liver.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Peanuts contain oxalates, which may be a concern for people prone to kidney stones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peanuts can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, or processed into peanut butter. Roasted salted peanuts are popular as a snack, while boiled peanuts feature in many Asian dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peanuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard any nuts with a rancid or off smell.

pinto-beans-from-canned-no-added-fat.title: Pinto Beans, Canned, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans, canned with no added fat, are a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected dry pinto beans that are cooked and sealed without oil or salt. Pinto beans have a mild nutty flavor, a soft texture, and provide a good source of plant protein, fiber, and micronutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pinto beans originated in Mexico and are a staple in Latin American cuisine.
Dry pinto beans require long soaking, but the canned version is ready straight from the jar.
Pinto beans are rich in antioxidants, including polyphenols that help combat free radicals.
Canning without added fat preserves the beans' natural taste and makes them a lower‑calorie option.
They are commonly used in chili, soups, salads, and vegetarian dishes.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: A typical serving (about 130 g) provides roughly 7 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and supports heart health.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes this product suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is important for DNA synthesis and is especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Sodium in the brine
items.content: Although no fat is added, the packing liquid may contain salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gas in sensitive people; introduce them gradually into the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned pinto beans are ready to eat straight from the jar. Add them to salads, soups, chili, tacos, or use as a filling for burritos. For a warm dish, briefly sauté with vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer beans to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for 3–4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet and sour shrimp is a dish made with large peeled shrimp that are quickly stir‑fried and coated in a tangy sauce made from vinegar, sugar, soy sauce, tomato paste, and spices. The result is a bright balance of sweetness and mild acidity, crisp shrimp texture, and a hint of heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sweet‑and‑sour sauce originated in Chinese cuisine and became popular in the United States in the mid‑20th century.
Shrimp are one of the fastest‑growing seafood species, requiring less water and feed than many land‑based animals.
Traditional recipes often include pineapple, but many modern versions use only the sauce without fruit.
The dish is commonly served over rice or noodles to balance its bold flavors.
The sauce can be adapted for vegetarians by substituting tofu for shrimp.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Shrimp provide a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other protein sources, shrimp contain relatively little saturated fat.

items.title: Rich in selenium
items.content: Selenium supports immune function and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Shrimp are a good source of vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish also provides zinc and iron, which are vital for healthy blood formation.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and other sauce ingredients can raise sodium levels, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne pathogens
items.content: Improperly stored shrimp can harbor bacteria that cause food poisoning.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically in individual plates. Shrimp can be enjoyed on their own or paired with rice, noodles, or a vegetable side. Garnish with fresh cilantro, sliced green onions, or toasted sesame seeds for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked sweet and sour shrimp in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. If frozen, keep for up to 1 month. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.
